Hip Abductor Tendon (Gluteus Medius and Minimus) Injuries
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Increasingly recognized as a common cause of greater trochanteric pain syndrome
Described as the rotator cuff tears of the hip
Can be intrasubstance, partial-thickness, or full-thickness tears

Overview
The gluteus medius and minimus are similar to the rotator cuff of the shoulder in that
they stabilize the joint (in this case, the hip) while providing rotation and assisting in
abduction.1 Patients with these tears often present with lateral hip pain, a
Trendelenburg gait, and weakness or pain with abduction. Typically, tears are initially
managed nonsurgically; patients experiencing recalcitrant pain or symptoms may be
indicated for surgical repair, which can be performed endoscopically or via an open
approach. After surgical treatment, patients experience favorable outcomes and
functional improvement at short-term follow-up.
Epidemiology
Most injuries occur in patients older than 50 years but have been reported in teenage patients.
More prevalent in females
Typically present as chronic tears
Can occur insidiously or traumatically

Abductor tendon tears are more common in females. They have been shown to have a
peak incidence between 50 and 70 years of age, with the prevalence of tears being 25%
for women and 10% for men in this age range.2
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The gluteus medius and minimus tendons insert onto the greater trochanter.
The gluteus medius has three distinct portions: anterior, middle, and posterior.
Both muscles receive blood supply from the superior gluteal artery and are innervated by the
superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1).

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The origin of the gluteus medius spans from the anterior superior iliac spine to the outer
edge of the iliac crest and back to the posterior superior iliac spine.3 The muscle is
composed of three distinct portions: anterior, middle, and posterior. The anterior and
middle portions are oriented vertically and aid in initiating hip abduction, whereas the
posterior portion is oriented horizontally and stabilizes the hip during gait.3 The gluteus
medius tendon has two distinct insertion sites on the greater trochanter. All of the
anterior and some of the central portions of the muscle insert onto the lateral facet, and
the posterior portion inserts on the superoposterior facet4 (Resource 1; Figure 1). The
origin of the gluteus minimus spans from the anterior inferior iliac (AIIS) spine to the
posterior inferior iliac spine. It runs parallel to the femoral neck and inserts into the hip
capsule and the lateral facet of the greater trochanter beneath the gluteus medius.5 The
gluteus minimus and the posterior gluteus medius stabilize the femoral head within the
acetabulum during gait.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Abductor tendon tears are caused or noticed in three common clinical scenarios. The
first is a chronic, atraumatic tear of the anterior fibers of the gluteus medius and
minimus tendons, which was described by Kagan6 as the rotator cuff tear of the hip. The
second is a tear discovered during total hip arthroplasty to repair a femoral neck
fracture. In a case series of consecutive patients who underwent total hip arthroplasty

Injury Classification
Tears can be divided into chronic tendinosis, partial-thickness, and full thickness-tears.
The Milwaukee classification is based on tear size.
One classification system is based on intraoperative findings.
A new classification system was introduced in 2020.
The Fuchs modification of the Goutallier classification for rotator cuff tears has been applied to
abductor tendon tears.

Injury Classification
The Milwaukee classification system is based on the hours of a clock face. On the right
hip from posterior to anterior, the gluteus medius inserts between the 11-o’clock and 3-
o’clock positions. On the left hip, the gluteus medius inserts between 9-o’clock and 1-
o’clock positions. The grade of the tear is based on how many hours the tear spans, with
grade 4 representing a bald trochanter (eg, a tear from the 1-o’clock to 3-o’clock
positions would be grade 2).10,11

Type 1 tears have a normal bursa, normal appearance of the gluteus medius tendon,
deep surface detachment anteriorly only, and a normal gluteus minimus.
Type 2 tears have a normal bursa, thickening of the tendon, grayish discoloration, loss
of normal striations, detachment that may extend posteriorly, and a stretched gluteus
minimus.
Type 3 tears have a scarred bursa and may have free fluid and tendon changes, as in
type 2 tears, but a small disruption exposing the underlying trochanter with a partial
tear or detachment of the gluteus minimus.
Type 4 tears have total disruption of the gluteus medius and minimus tendons,
exposing the entire trochanter front and back, with ulceration of the fascia lata.
Incavo and Harper13 developed a new classification system with two types.
Type I has no evidence of gluteus medius avulsion from bone and has three subtypes.
Subtype A: partial tear of the gluteus minimus or gluteus medius tendon
Subtype B: complete tear of the gluteus minimus tendon
Subtype C: longitudinal tear of the gluteus medius tendon
Type II displays evidence of a gluteus medius avulsion and has two subtypes.
Subtype A: avulsion of less than 50% of the greater trochanter insertion
Subtype B: avulsion of greater than or equal to 50% of the greater trochanter
insertion.
The Goutallier/Fuchs classification system can be applied to abductor tendon tears and
assesses the fatty infiltration and muscle quality of the gluteus medius and minimus.
This should be evaluated via coronal T1-weighted MRIs without fat suppression. Grading
is as follows: grade 0 has normal muscle, grade 1 has muscle with some fatty streaks,
grade 2 has fatty infiltration but more muscle than fat, grade 3 has equal amounts of
muscle and fat, and grade 4 has more fat than muscle.14

Patient History and Physical Examination
A thorough history and physical examination in patients with lateral hip pain are required.
Patients usually present with a dull pain on the lateral aspect of the hip.

The pain is aggravated by pressure on the area, weight bearing, and resisted hip abduction.
Muscles and tendons should be palpated from their origins to their insertions on the greater
trochanter.
Strength of abduction must be assessed.
Special tests include the Trendelenburg test, the double- to single-leg stance test, the supine
and lateral decubitus hip abduction tests, and the hip-lag sign test.
The patient may exhibit a Trendelenburg gait, in which the patient experiences a drooping of
the pelvis on the contralateral side.

Patient History and Physical Examination
A thorough history is indicated for patients who have lateral-sided hip pain. The
presentation of these tears may vary, but patients often experience lateral hip pain that
is aggravated with palpation and resisted abduction. Surgical history of the hip must be
noted. The physical examination is equally important, and strength of abduction must be
noted. Examination of gait may demonstrate an antalgic gait or a Trendelenburg gait (ie,
abductor lurch; Resource 2; Figure 2). A Trendelenburg gait results from a defective hip
abductor mechanism that causes the drooping of the pelvis on the contralateral side of
the injured hip. A Trendelenburg test can be performed with the physician standing
behind the patient and observing if the patient’s contralateral pelvis drops as he or she
lifts the injured lower extremity.15 The double-to single-leg stance test is performed in a
similar manner, with the physician observing for pelvic tilt or lateral shifting of the hip
while standing behind the patient as he or she raises one leg from a double-leg stance.
The side-lying hip abduction test, which is more difficult for the patient to perform than
the supine test, allows physicians to note subtle weakness of the affected hip.
In addition, the hip-lag sign test should be performed because research has shown that
a positive test finding is substantially correlated with hip abductor injuries.16 To perform
this test, the patient is instructed to lie on the side with the affected extremity on top.
The top knee is flexed 45°; the physician passively moves the hip into 10° of extension,
20° of abduction, and maximal internal rotation and instructs the patient to hold this
position. If the foot drops more than 10 cm, then the test finding is positive. Lastly, the
physician should perform the modified resisted internal rotation test. The patient lies

Imaging Studies
The imaging modality most widely used to diagnose abductor tendon tears, which often
manifest with trochanteric bursitis, is MRI.3 MRI allows surgeons to determine if a tear is
partial or full thickness and should always be performed to confirm the diagnosis.
Cvitanic et al20 reported that MRI was accurate in 91% of patients with regard to the
diagnosis of abductor tendon tears when compared with intraoperative findings. The
authors also reported that T2-weighted images with an area of hyperintensity superior
to the greater trochanter had a sensitivity of 73% and a specificity of 95% for the
diagnosis of hip abductor tendon tears (Figure 3). Overall, the authors found that
positive and negative predictive values for diagnosing hip abductor tendon tears were
79% and 95%, respectively.20

pain syndrome, such as greater trochanteric bursitis and external coxa sultans.5

Torres et al24 performed a systematic review and described a stepwise approach to the
nonsurgical management of greater trochanteric pain syndrome. The authors suggested
that initial therapy should include rest, heat/ice, and the use of NSAIDs. If patients fail to
respond to these therapies, corticosteroid injections or shockwave therapy should be
considered. If those modalities fail, PRP may be considered next (Video 1). A double-
blinded randomized controlled trial comparing the effectiveness of a single leukocyte-
rich PRP injection versus a corticosteroid injection in patients with chronic gluteal
tendinopathy demonstrated greater improvement in pain and function in the group who
received the leukocyte-rich PRP, and this improvement was sustained at 2-year follow-
up. The group who received the corticosteroid injection achieved maximal improvement,
but they did not maintain functional improvement beyond 24 weeks.25,26 The use of PRP
is controversial in the literature, with some doubt concerning its efficacy. Harper et al27
provided an overview of the management of hip abductor tears and recalcitrant
trochanteric bursitis in native hips.

Surgical Management
Indications
Failed nonsurgical management
Recalcitrant pain or symptoms in patients with a known abductor tendon tear
Contraindications
Cigarette smoking
Medical comorbidities
Techniques/Procedures
Repair may be performed endoscopically or via an open procedure, with the decision being
based on size, retraction, and degree of muscle atrophy and fatty infiltration associated with
the tear.
Partial-thickness tears can be repaired endoscopically.
Open repair may be indicated for full-thickness tears with tendon retraction, substantial fatty
atrophy, or both.
A massive irreparable tear may require an open gluteus maximus muscle transfer or
augmented repair.
Suture anchor is placed in the greater trochanter via single- or double-row repair.
Concomitant gluteus maximus transfer or allograft augmentation may be indicated for the
management of massive tears or those with considerable fatty infiltration and muscle atrophy.
Preoperative Planning
MRIs should be reviewed to determine tendon involvement, the degree of tearing, and the
degree of fatty infiltration.
Severity of tearing is a deciding factor for pursuing an open or endoscopic approach.
Patient Positioning
Patient positioning depends on surgical technique.
For endoscopic repair, the patient is positioned on a standard traction table with a hip
distraction station and a perineal post.


Patient Positioning
In patients undergo endoscopic repair, the feet are securely fastened in padded boots
and the pelvis is translated toward the unaffected hip. For open procedures, patients are
placed in the lateral decubitus position and secured with the use of well-padded hip
positioners or a peg board. All bony prominences are padded, and a pneumatic
compression device is placed on the nonsurgical leg.
Surgical Approaches
For endoscopic repair, anterolateral, mid-anterior, and posterolateral portals are
established,28 and a 70° arthroscope is used.29
For open repair, a direct lateral approach with a lateral skin incision centered over the greater
trochanter is used.5
In both techniques, a trochanteric bursectomy is performed.

Surgical Approaches
The anterolateral portal is established 1 cm anterior and 1 cm proximal to the anterior
aspect of the greater trochanter. A mid-anterior portal is established 4 to 5 cm medial
and 1 cm inferior to the anterolateral portal. Lastly, a posterolateral portal is established
1 cm posterior and 1 cm proximal to the posterolateral aspect of the greater trochanter.
In open repair, a lateral incision centered over the greater trochanter that is
approximately 6 to 8 cm in length is made (Figure 4). This incision is used to develop the
interval between subcutaneous tissue and the underlying iliotibial band. Next, the
iliotibial band is split longitudinally in line with its fibers. This allows access into the
peritrochanteric space after retractors are placed.

Tendon Repair
In open repair, residual soft-tissue remnants are thoroughly débrided off the footprint on the
greater trochanter to promote a favorable healing response.
A burr is used to débride the bony bed of the hip abductor tendon insertions until healthy
bleeding bone is encountered, with care taken to preserve a sufficient amount of cortical bone
to promote time-zero fixation.
Gluteus medius and minimus tendons are identified.
Suture anchors are placed at the peripheral zones of the footprint.
Double-row fixation or transosseous-equivalent configurations can be used.
In patients with an irreparable tear, concomitant gluteus maximus transfer, augmented repair,
or reconstruction may be performed (Figure 5).

In endoscopic repair, after all portals are established, the hip is placed in extension and 15° to
20° of abduction with maximum internal rotation of the foot.
An arthroscope is inserted into the mid-anterior portal for visualization of the peritrochanteric
space.
A known gluteus medius tear will commonly involve the entire lateral footprint.
A bubble test can help identify undersurface (partial articular gluteal tendon avulsion) tears.
The footprint is decorticated to promote healing.
Suture anchors are placed after proper tension of the abductor tendons is confirmed.
A double-row suture bridge may be necessary for large or retracted tears.
Postoperative Management
Avoidance of tension on repaired musculotendinous unit

Postoperative Management
No standard postoperative protocol is available for use after surgical repair of the
abductor tendon. The goal of postoperative management is to reduce tension on the
tendon to allow for optimal healing. Patients are fitted with a hip brace to prevent
passive adduction and active hip abduction, and a Trendelenburg gait should be
avoided. Patients are instructed to use crutches and remain partial–weight bearing for 6
to 8 weeks postoperatively. Some surgeons recommend the use of a continuous passive
motion machine for the first 3 weeks postoperatively, and most surgeons recommend
the use of a stationary bicycle. A rehabilitation program focuses on core strengthening
and proximal neuromotor control, including proprioceptive and perturbation training. At
12 weeks postoperatively, the patient may progress to abductor strengthening and
progressive return to activity is permitted.
Complications

Complications
A recent systematic review showed that endoscopic repair resulted in complication rates
lower than those of open repair and that the most common complications associated
with open repair were re-tears (4.5% to 25.0%), hematoma (zero to 3.4%), and deep
infection (zero to 6.3%).11
Outcomes
Open and endoscopic approaches result in favorable outcomes.
Open procedures may be associated with higher complication rates.

Outcomes
Patients generally have favorable outcomes after open repair of the abductor tendons.
Walsh et al12 evaluated 72 patients at a minimum 12-month follow-up and reported that
90% of the patients were pain-free or had substantial improvements in pain compared
with their preoperative levels. Davies et al30 reported an improvement in Harris Hip
scores at a minimum 5-year follow-up. Three of the 19 patients had poor results, and
poor results were more common in patients with the largest tears.
In a systematic review, Chandrasekaran et al11 compared patients who underwent open
versus endoscopic repair of abductor muscle tears and found similar outcomes between
the techniques. Patients in both groups had improvement in functional outcome scores,
pain, and hip abduction strength. Voos et al31 reported one of the earliest case series on
endoscopic gluteus medius tendon repair, reported that all patients had improvement in
pain and abduction strength at mean follow-up of 25 months. In a case series of 15
patients, Domb et al32 showed that 14 patients had improvement in all hip-specific
functional outcome scores at a mean follow-up of 27.9 months. Hartigan et al33 found
substantial improvements in patient-reported outcome scores at a mean of 38 months
after endoscopic repair of partial-thickness undersurface gluteal tears. Perets et al34

In a recent meta-analysis of 206 repairs, Looney et al36 reported that high-grade fatty
infiltration was associated with less improvement in function based on the modified
Harris Hip score but similar improvement in pain. In patients with a massive tear or
severe fatty infiltration, an augment or reconstruction may be indicated. This is a
relatively new technique, and limited evidence supports surgical management of
abductor tendon tears involving the use of synthetic, allograft, and autograft tissue for
augmentation or reconstruction. The available case series demonstrate promising
results. Fehm et al37 used Achilles tendon allograft for reconstruction in seven patients
and showed substantial improvements in pain, limp, and abduction strength. In a larger
case series of 142 patients, Ebert et al38 performed augmentation with the use of a
transosseous synthetic scaffold and demonstrated substantial improvement in
functional outcomes at 2-year follow-up. Davies et al30 used a dermal allograft for
augmentation and reported improvement in outcome scores at 1 and 5 years
postoperatively. Rao et al39 also used an allograft dermal matrix in a case series of 12
patients and showed substantial improvements in pain, abductor strength, gait function,
and functional outcome scores at a mean follow-up of 22 months. Lemme et al40
reported improved patient-reported outcomes after gluteus medius/minimus repair
augmentation or reconstruction via gluteus maximus transfer.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Hip abductor tendon injuries occur most commonly in patients older than 50 years, but they
also have been reported in teenage patients.
Increasingly recognized as a common cause of greater trochanteric pain syndrome
Commonly chronic, atraumatic tear
Patients experience dull pain over the lateral aspect of the hip and may have weakness with

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The direct (straight) head of the rectus femoris originates from the AIIS, whereas the indirect
(reflected) head of the rectus femoris originates slightly posterior and inferior to the superior
acetabular ridge and the hip joint capsule.84
The rectus femoris is innervated by the femoral nerve.
The AIIS is a bony prominence superior to the acetabulum.
The rectus femoris crosses the hip joint and the knee joint and joins the remainder of the
quadriceps on the patellar tendon.

Management
Nonsurgical Management
These injuries are most often managed nonsurgically via rest, ice, and activity modifications.
Indications for nonsurgical management
Proximal avulsion with minimal displacement (<2 cm)
Musculotendinous tears with no to minimal retraction (<2 cm)
Patients who are sedentary or are low-level athletes with acceptable function
Nonsurgical management includes a graduated rehabilitation program with the goal of
returning to sports activity; proximal rectus femoris injuries are associated with a longer
recovery period than distal tears.
90
AIIS avulsions
The hip is flexed for 2 weeks followed by guarded–weight bearing to prevent tension at the
muscle origin.
After immobilization, patients should complete a formal rehabilitation program involving
passive mobilization, strength training, and neuromuscular control of the injured lower
extremity. A return-to-sport protocol involving sport-specific exercises should be followed
after the patient is able.91
Surgical Management
Indications for surgical management81,92
High-level athletes with displacement greater than >2 cm
Failed nonsurgical management with continued pain or weakness.
Preoperatively, the physician should review MRIs to assess the degree of tearing and the
degree of retraction.
The patient is placed in the supine position on a standard surgical table.
The anterior approach to the hip (Smith-Petersen) is used to access the rectus femoris.
Care should be taken to avoid the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.
The tendon is prepared for repair via débridement of devitalized tissue.
A bony bleeding bed is created at the tendon footprint to aid healing.
The tendon is reattached to the footprint with the use of suture anchors.81,93,94
Sonnery-Cottet et al92 recommended surgical excision of the avulsed tendon followed by
muscular suture repair.

Outcomes
Nonsurgical and surgical treatment are associated with favorable results.
Gamradt et al85 examined 11 professional football players who underwent nonsurgical
treatment and found that 10 patients returned to sports activity at a mean of 55.3 days, with
the last patient returning to sports activity at 7 months.
Recurrence of symptoms occurred in 2 of the 11 patients at final follow-up.
In a small case series of two professional football kickers treated nonsurgically, both patients
were able to return to sports activity at 3 months postoperatively.99
In a case series of 10 professional soccer players who underwent surgical repair of the rectus
femoris tendon augmented with PRP, patients returned to play at an mean of 3.8 months
postoperatively without complications.
Irmola et al94 observed five elite-level athletes who underwent surgical repair and reported
that the patients returned to sports activity at their preinjury level at 5 to 10 months
postoperatively.
Sonnery-Cottet et al92 performed surgical excision of the proximal rectus tendon in five
professional soccer players. Patients returned to sports activity at a mean of 15 weeks
postoperatively. At 3 months postoperatively, patients scored 16/16 on the Marx Activity
Rating Scale and 80/80 on the Lower Extremity Functional Scale.
Kayani et al100 compared primary repair versus proximal rectus tenodesis and reported no
differences in patient satisfaction, functional outcome scores, and quadriceps muscle strength
between the treatment groups at 1- and 2-year follow-up.
AIIS avulsions
Patients with AIIS avulsions treated nonsurgically have great outcomes, with return to sports
activity at previous levels.46,89,96
In patients in whom nonsurgical treatment fails and who undergo arthroscopic or open
fixation of the fracture, pain is greatly decreased at follow-up, and patients are able to return
to sports activity at full function.88,97

Pearls and Pitfalls
Rectus femoris injuries range from musculotendinous junction injuries to avulsions.
Rectus avulsions are rare injuries that occur in athletes who participate in sports that require
explosive movements or kicking.
Typically, patients exhibit anterior hip pain and may have weakness with hip flexion.
These injuries usually are managed nonsurgically. Surgical repair is indicated in patients in
whom nonsurgical treatment fails, patients with an avulsion with greater than 2 cm of
retraction, and high-level athletes.
Nonsurgical and surgical management are associated with good outcomes, with patients being
able to return to sports activity quickly and at the same level.
